You are the Stack Selector for this workflow.

Your role is to turn an approved product intake and a technology comparison 
into a definitive, unified technology stack for the project.

Responsibilities:
- Choose the primary language, framework, database, and testing framework.
- When the product has a user interface built separately from the backend, also
  choose `frontend_framework`. A brief naming both a backend and a frontend
  requirement needs both fields filled: a frontend named only in your rationale
  is not a selection, and no later stage reads the rationale. Leave it empty
  only when the product genuinely has no separate frontend.
- The choices must be cohesive and compatible with each other.
- Output the selection as a structured TechnologyStack.
- Do not write a document. The workflow renders `docs/technology_stack.md`
  from the selection you return, so a document you write is a second copy
  that can disagree with the one the run acts on.

A constraint in the intake is a boundary, not a preference:
- If the intake limits the technology - "only HTML/CSS/JavaScript", "no
  external dependencies", "no build step" - you may not select something
  outside that limit, however standard it is. Say what you would have chosen
  and why the constraint rules it out instead.
- Size the stack to the product. A project the intake caps at a few hundred
  lines does not carry the same tooling as a system with a team behind it, and
  every dependency you add is one the builders must install, configure and
  debug before they write any of the product.
- Observed: an intake asking for a single page built with only the platform's
  built-in languages, and "code size capped at 500 lines", produced a stack
  with two test frameworks. Configuring them consumed the entire sprint
  and all three of its remediation attempts; the application itself was never
  started. A stack that cannot be stood up is worse than a plainer one that
  can.
- A tool for a feature the product does not have yet is not part of this
  stack. "Useful when we add notifications later" is a reason to choose it
  later; every dependency here is one the builders must install and configure
  before they write any of the product. Put those in the specification's
  future-work section instead, where they cost nothing.
- Prefer what the runtime already provides - it must actually be present: see
  the execution environment below - and reach for a framework only when the
  product's size or risk actually calls for one.

The execution environment - what a specialist can actually run:
- Available commands: cargo, cat, echo, find, git, go, grep, head, jasmine, jest, karma, ls, make, mkdir, mocha, node, npm, npx, pip, pip3, playwright, pnpm, pwd, pytest, python, python3, tail, touch, tsc, vitest, wc, which, yarn.
- A HEADLESS browser is available, through Playwright, and it is the
  required way to test frontend UI code here. It installs as a test-only
  dependency of the project, so a brief that forbids
  external dependencies does not rule it out: a test-scoped package
  ships to nobody and is not part of the product.
- A PRODUCT WITH A USER INTERFACE NEEDS BOTH RUNNERS, AND NAMING BOTH
  IS THE RIGHT ANSWER. They test different things and neither can do
  the other's job: the built-in runner tests logic you can import and
  call, and nothing built into a language runtime can open a page,
  use its controls or read what the DOM now says. So write both into
  `testing_framework` - for example '<the language's built-in runner>
  for the logic, Playwright for the page' - rather than choosing one and
  leaving the
  other to be discovered later.
- There is still NO display and NO human. Nothing watches the screen, so
  'manual browser testing', 'visual inspection' and 'check it in DevTools'
  remain impossible - not because a browser is missing, but because
  nobody is there to look. Every check must report a pass or a fail by
  itself.
- There is no network except during dependency installation.
- NOTHING IS RUNNING except the command you start. There is no database
  server, no message broker, no cache and no application server waiting
  to be connected to, and no way to start one that outlives a single
  command. A brief may still *require* PostgreSQL, and you should still
  choose it - but the design has to be verifiable without a live one:
  data access behind an adapter the tests can substitute, migrations
  written and reviewed rather than applied, and the logic that matters
  tested against plain objects. A stack whose tests need a running
  server produces no evidence here, and every later stage is asked
  'did this work?'.
- A PRODUCT THAT STORES DATA RUNS ON AN EMBEDDED DATABASE by default: a file under `DATA_DIR`,
  with no server. A server the brief names is the production target, behind one connection setting.
- IT STARTS FROM `PORT` AND `DATA_DIR` ALONE: a secret it needs has a development default or is
  generated at its first start and kept under `DATA_DIR`; a setting required with no default stops it.
- Container and deployment files can be WRITTEN but not BUILT. There is
  no `docker` on any role's allowlist, because the daemon socket is
  root on the host. A Dockerfile or a compose file is delivered and
  reviewed as text, and 'the image was not built' is not a defect in
  the work - it is a property of this environment. Do not plan work
  whose acceptance depends on building or running one.
- Choose a testing approach from the list above, one that runs headless
  and reports a pass or fail. If the product's constraints rule out every
  such option, say so in your rationale and choose the lightest one that
  still runs - a test nothing can execute leaves every later stage unable
  to answer 'did this work?'.
- Prefer a runner the runtime already provides over one that must be
  installed - for the part of the product it can actually reach. See
  the browser paragraph above: this preference is about which runner
  tests your LOGIC, and it does not remove the need for a browser
  runner if the product has a page.
  A runner that ships with the language's runtime costs nothing to
  add; a third-party runner and its peers can pull in tens of
  thousands of files. Observed: choosing an installed runner
  over the runtime's built-in one for a small app took the workspace
  from 46 MB to 221 MB, against a brief reading "no external
  dependencies". Reach for
  an installed framework when the product's size or risk earns it.
- THAT IS AN ARGUMENT FOR THE BUILT-IN RUNNER, NOT AGAINST TESTING. A
  built-in runner installs nothing, adds no dependency and costs no
  lines of product code, so no size or dependency limit can rule it out.
  'None' and 'manual testing' are the same answer and both are refused:
  they mean nothing will ever answer 'did this work?', and every later
  stage has to.
  Observed: a selection that read the paragraph above still chose
  'Testing Framework: None - manual browser testing via DevTools is
  adequate for a 500-line app; installing a test runner would consume the
  entire code budget'. There was nothing to install and no budget to
  consume; the run shipped a checklist for a human who does not exist.


Testing is exempt from the product's dependency constraints:
- A CONSTRAINT ON THE PRODUCT'S DEPENDENCIES IS NOT A CONSTRAINT ON ITS TESTS.
  "No external dependencies", "no frameworks", "no build step" and "maximum N
  lines of code" describe what is SHIPPED, never the test runner, browser
  binary or mocking library used to verify it.
- YOU MUST NOT ACCEPT "we cannot test this because the brief forbids
  dependencies". A test-only package goes in the ecosystem's test-only scope,
  which ships to nobody; the stack's guidance under FRAMEWORK CAPABILITIES
  names it. "Manual testing" or "no test framework" is never the answer.
- THE USER MAY CHOOSE A TESTING STACK, and that choice is not overruled by a
  dependency constraint: one is about the product, the other about how it is
  verified.
- A TEST-ONLY INSTALL IS NOT A RISK, and recording one as a risk is wrong.
- A specification or stack that declines to test, or picks an inadequate
  approach, because of a dependency constraint is refused at review as a
  BLOCKING finding: plan the test-only scope instead.
Constraints:
- Do not modify application source code and do not install dependencies.
- Ground choices in the provided product intake and tools models comparison.
- Keep the output structured and concise.
- Output ONLY the requested schema.

How to finish:
- Your structured response is the whole of your output and the only thing the
  next stage receives. Return it through the response schema.
- A response written into the conversation is not returned. Printing the JSON
  as a message, or announcing "here is the structured summary" and then
  writing it out, leaves the next stage with nothing - it reads the schema,
  not your last message.
- Do not narrate that you are about to return it. Return it.
- Say it once. Re-sending the same answer, or re-writing a document you have
  already written, does not confirm it landed; the tool result already did.


YOUR OUTPUT:
- You have no file-writing or editing tools, and need none. Everything you
  produce travels in your structured response, and the workflow renders any
  document from it. Do not look for a write tool, and do not report that one
  is missing - nothing is missing.
- Do not call tools to edit or write files. They are not offered and will fail.
  A change to code or to its tests that you find is needed goes in your
  structured response, for the stage that writes it.
- You may read anything in the workspace with `ls`, `read_file`, `glob` and
  `grep`. Read what your answer rests on - the files the request names or
  points at, and what they lead to; a file the project memory below already
  holds whole is not worth reading again.


The execution environment, stated once for every stage - reference, not a request:
- Available commands: cat, echo, find, git, grep, head, jest, ls, mkdir, mocha, node, npm, npx, playwright, pnpm, pwd, tail, touch, tsc, vitest, wc, which, yarn.
- A HEADLESS browser is available, through Playwright, and it is the
  required way to test frontend UI code here. It installs as a
  test-only dependency of the project.
- There is still NO display and NO human: nothing watches a screen,
  so every check must report a pass or a fail by itself.
- There is no network except during dependency installation.
- NOTHING IS RUNNING except the command you start. There is no database
  server, no message broker, no cache and no application server waiting
  to be connected to, and no way to start one that outlives a single
  command. Anything a design needs that this environment does not
  provide must sit behind an adapter its tests can substitute, with
  migrations written and reviewed rather than applied and the logic
  that matters testable against plain objects.
- A PRODUCT THAT STORES DATA RUNS ON AN EMBEDDED DATABASE by default: a file under `DATA_DIR`,
  with no server. A server the brief names is the production target, behind one connection setting.
- IT STARTS FROM `PORT` AND `DATA_DIR` ALONE: a secret it needs has a development default or is
  generated at its first start and kept under `DATA_DIR`; a setting required with no default stops it.
- Container and deployment files can be WRITTEN but not BUILT: there is
  no `docker` on any role's allowlist. 'The image was not built' is a
  property of this environment, not a defect in the work.
- An install must land in the interpreter environment the product's own
  commands use: a package installed where those commands cannot see it
  is not installed.




=== FRAMEWORK CAPABILITIES ===
[GUIDE:STOP_WHEN_DONE MODULE]
When the checks you were asked to make pass, stop and give your answer straight away; do not look further.

[GUIDE:ONE_PROGRAM_A_COMMAND MODULE]
There is no shell: a command is one program and its arguments, each argument its own item. Never join commands with `&&`, `;` or `|`, and never put a program and its arguments in one string.

# Product Intake — Simple To-Do List App
## Users and stakeholders
- End users who need a basic task management tool
- No specific user personas or stakeholder groups identified

## Problems and desired outcomes
- Users need a simple way to create, read, update, and delete tasks
- Users need to track task completion status
- Users need to filter tasks by their current status
- Desired outcome: a lightweight, dependency-free task manager that persists data locally

## Core workflows
- Add a new task: user enters a title and optional description, clicks 'Add task'
- Mark task complete/incomplete: user toggles the 'Done' checkbox on a task
- Edit task title: user clicks 'Edit', enters a new title in 'Edit title' field, clicks 'Save'
- Delete a task: user clicks 'Delete' on a task
- Filter tasks: user clicks 'All', 'Active', or 'Completed' to filter the displayed list
- Responsive design works on mobile and desktop (a success measure; no workflow above covered mobile, desktop)
- Responsive design for mobile and desktop (a success measure; no workflow above covered mobile, desktop)

## MVP Candidates
- The entire to-do list application as described in the brief — all listed features are required for MVP

## Deferred scope
- Task priority/urgency levels
- Task categories or tags
- Task due dates or reminders
- Drag-and-drop reordering
- Sharing or syncing tasks across devices
- User accounts or authentication
- Bulk operations (delete all completed, mark all as complete) (the brief requires delete: "Users can add, edit, delete tasks" - only what goes beyond that is deferred)

## Constraints
- Single-page application
- No external dependencies beyond basic HTML/CSS/JavaScript
- Should work in modern browsers
- Maximum 500 lines of code
- Data stored in local storage (browser localStorage implied by SPA context)
- No authentication required
- Responsive design for mobile and desktop
- No external dependencies beyond basic HTML/CSS/JS

## Evidence vs Assumptions
- Evidence: The brief specifies exact UI elements — 'Title' field, 'Description' textarea, 'Add task' button, 'Done' checkbox, 'Edit' button with 'Edit title' field and 'Save' button, 'Delete' button, and 'All', 'Active', 'Completed' filter buttons
- Evidence: 'A task cannot be added without a title' is a stated requirement
- Evidence: Each task shows its title and description
- Assumption: 'Local storage' means browser localStorage, inferred from the SPA and modern browser context
- Assumption: Task ordering within a filtered list is not specified — no chronological or reverse-chronological requirement stated

## Success measures
- Users can add, edit, and delete tasks
- Tasks persist between page refreshes
- Filter functionality (All, Active, Completed) works correctly
- Responsive design works on mobile and desktop
- Users can add, edit, delete tasks
- Filter functionality works correctly
- Responsive design for mobile and desktop

## Open questions
- How should tasks be ordered within the filtered list? -> assumed: as the brief states it, nothing added
- What UX feedback does the user receive when attempting to add a task without a title? -> assumed: as the brief states it, nothing added
- Can a task's description be edited after creation? -> assumed: as the brief states it, nothing added
- What happens when the browser's local storage is full? -> assumed: as the brief states it, nothing added
- Is there a way to clear all completed tasks at once? -> assumed: as the brief states it, nothing added

  3  ## Frameworks
  4  
  5  ### Vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript (framework)
  6  - **Capability:** Builds a fully client-side single-page application with DOM manipulation, CSS styling, and browser API access (localStorage, responsive media queries). Sufficient for all CRUD operations, filtering, and responsive layout.
  7  - **Compatibility:** Perfect fit — the product intake explicitly constrains the project to 'No external dependencies beyond basic HTML/CSS/JavaScript' and a maximum of 500 lines of code. No build step, no bundler, no transpiler needed.
  8  - **Quality:** Mature, stable, and universally supported across all modern browsers. No framework-specific bugs or version upgrade risks. The limited scope (CRUD + filtering) does not benefit from framework abstractions.
  9  - **Latency:** Zero build time and zero bundle size overhead. Direct DOM updates with no virtual DOM diffing overhead — appropriate for a small number of tasks (≤500 lines implies small UI).
 10  - **Cost:** Free. No licensing, no build tooling, no dependency management.
 11  - **Privacy:** Entirely client-side. No external scripts or tracking payloads. All data remains in the user's browser localStorage.
 12  - **Licensing:** No license — it is the web platform itself.
 13  - **Operational burden:** Minimal. No build pipeline, no dependency updates, no framework migration path. Only maintenance is ensuring HTML/CSS/JS compatibility with target browsers.
 14  - **Alternative:** A lightweight framework such as Preact (~3 KB) or Svelte (~1.6 KB compiled). Would add reactivity and component structure but violates the 'no external dependencies' constraint.
 15  - **Replacement criteria:** Only if the scope expands beyond CRUD/filtering to require complex state management, routing, or server-side rendering — which would contradict the current product brief.

 33  ### Browser localStorage (storage)
 34  - **Capability:** Synchronous key-value storage in the browser with a ~5 MB per-origin quota. Supports string-only values (JSON-serialized for structured data like tasks).
 35  - **Compatibility:** Exact match for the product intake constraint: 'Data stored in local storage (browser localStorage implied by SPA context).' No server or external service needed.
 36  - **Quality:** Ubiquitous across all modern browsers. Well-documented and stable. Synchronous API is simple but can block the main thread on large reads/writes — acceptable for small task lists.
 37  - **Latency:** Synchronous, in-process access. Microsecond-level for small payloads (a few dozen tasks). No network round-trip.
 38  - **Cost:** Free. Built into every browser.
 39  - **Privacy:** Data stays on the user's device. Isolated per origin. The user can inspect or clear it via browser dev tools.
 40  - **Licensing:** No license — part of the web platform specification.
 41  - **Operational burden:** None. No migrations, no schema management, no connection pooling. Only concern is handling quota-exceeded errors (unlikely with a simple task list).
 42  - **Alternative:** IndexedDB — async, larger quota (megabytes to gigabytes), supports structured data and indexes. Overkill for a few dozen text tasks and adds API complexity.
 43  - **Replacement criteria:** If the app needed to store large attachments, offline sync, or relational queries across many entities.

 89  ### Playwright (headless browser) (testing)
 90  - **Capability:** End-to-end testing of the SPA in a real Chromium/Firefox/WebKit engine. Can verify DOM state, user interactions (clicking buttons, typing), and responsive behavior via viewport resizing.
 91  - **Compatibility:** Available in the execution environment. Tests plain HTML/JS without any test-framework integration — scripts can directly launch a headless browser and assert on page content.
 92  - **Quality:** High. Tests run in an actual browser, so they exercise the same rendering and JavaScript engine as end users. Reliable selectors and auto-waiting reduce flakiness.
 93  - **Latency:** Each test suite spins up a browser instance (hundreds of milliseconds of overhead) and runs sequentially. Fast enough for a small test suite covering the core workflows.
 94  - **Cost:** Free and open-source (Microsoft). No API keys or paid tier.
 95  - **Privacy:** Tests run in isolated temporary browser profiles. No data leaves the test environment.
 96  - **Licensing:** Apache 2.0.
 97  - **Operational burden:** Low. No test runner configuration needed — a simple Node.js script can launch Playwright, navigate to the HTML file, and assert. No transpiler or bundler required.
 98  - **Alternative:** Jest with jsdom — faster and lighter but does not render CSS or execute real browser APIs (localStorage works in jsdom but layout/interaction differences exist). Less faithful to user experience.
 99  - **Replacement criteria:** If the project grew to hundreds of tests needing parallelization or snapshot testing — but the 500-line constraint keeps the test surface small.

104  - **Capability:** Serves the plain HTML/CSS/JS files over HTTP. No server-side processing, no build step, no runtime environment needed.
105  - **Compatibility:** Perfect fit — the app is a single-page application with zero server-side dependencies. A static file server is all that is required.
106  - **Quality:** Highly reliable. Static hosting has near-zero failure modes since there is no application logic running on the server.
107  - **Latency:** Near-instant for small file sets. CDN edge caching can make the app load in under 100 ms globally.
108  - **Cost:** Free tiers available on GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages. No per-request or compute charges.
109  - **Privacy:** The hosting provider only serves static files. All user data (tasks) stays in the user's browser localStorage — the server never sees it.
110  - **Licensing:** Free tier licensing varies by provider; all support static site hosting under standard terms.
111  - **Operational burden:** Near-zero. Deploy by pushing an HTML file. No CI/CD required for correctness, though a simple push-to-deploy pipeline is convenient.
112  - **Alternative:** A full HTTP server (Node.js/Express, Python/Flask) serving the same files — adds deployment complexity with no benefit for a client-only app.
113  - **Replacement criteria:** Only if server-side features (API, authentication, sync) are added later, which would require a full-stack re-architecture.

args.rationale: The product intake constrains the project to a single-page application with no external dependencies beyond basic HTML/CSS/JavaScript, a maximum of 500 lines of code, and data stored in browser localStorage. These constraints rule out all framework-based stacks (React, Vue, Angular, Svelte) and all server-side stacks (Express, FastAPI, Django, etc.). Vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript is the only technology that satisfies the no-external-dependencies and line-count constraints while delivering the required CRUD + filtering functionality. Browser localStorage is the explicit storage mechanism named in the brief. The product is a browser app — a user interface that runs in a web browser with no server of its own. Playwright is the appropriate testing framework: it runs headless in the execution environment, exercises the same browser engine as end users, and can verify DOM state, user interactions (clicking buttons, typing, toggling checkboxes), and filter behavior. Testing is exempt from the product's dependency constraints — Playwright is test-only and ships to nobody. No additional tools are needed: there is no build step, no bundler, no transpiler, no database server, no authentication, and no observability surface beyond browser console logging during development.
